numberItems.stem: A shipper loaded and secured your trailer. Which of these are you still responsible for?
options: Nothing — the shipper is responsible for how it was loaded
Knowing the cargo does not restrict your access to emergency equipment
Only the paperwork, not the cargo itself
numberItems.explanation: Whether or not you loaded it, you must inspect the cargo, recognize overloads and poor balance, know it is secured and doesn't block your view, and know it doesn't restrict access to emergency equipment (p. 3-1).

numberItems.stem: You plan to haul HazMat that requires placards. What must you also have?
options: An "H" endorsement on your CDL
Nothing extra, if the shipper loaded it
A tank ("N") endorsement
numberItems.explanation: To carry HazMat that requires placards you also need an "H" endorsement (p. 3-1).

numberItems.stem: After you start a trip, you must inspect the cargo and its securing devices again within the first:
options: 100 miles
150 miles
50 miles
numberItems.explanation: Inspect the cargo and securing devices again within the first 50 miles after beginning a trip (p. 3-1).

numberItems.stem: After the first check, when must you inspect your cargo again during the trip?
options: Every 2 hours or 100 miles
After driving 3 hours or 150 miles, and after every break
Only after every break
numberItems.explanation: Re-inspect after you have driven 3 hours or 150 miles and after every break (p. 3-1).

numberItems.stem: A tractor, trailer and load are weighed together on a scale. That actual total weight is the:
options: Gross combination weight rating (GCWR)
Gross vehicle weight (GVW)
Gross combination weight (GCW)
numberItems.explanation: GCW is the total weight of a combination of vehicles including the load; the "R" (rating) terms are manufacturer values (p. 3-1).

numberItems.stem: The value the **manufacturer** specifies as the loaded weight of a combination vehicle is the:
options: Gross combination weight rating (GCWR)
Gross combination weight (GCW)
Gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR)
numberItems.explanation: GCWR is the manufacturer's specified loaded weight of a combination vehicle; GVWR is the same for a single vehicle (p. 3-1).

numberItems.stem: The manufacturer gives no GCWR for your combination. How is the GCWR found?
options: Add the GVWR of the power unit and the GVWR of the trailer
Add the GVWR of the power unit, the total weight of the towed unit, and any load on it
Use the actual scale weight of the tractor and trailer
numberItems.explanation: In the absence of a manufacturer value, GCWR = GVWR of the power unit + total weight of the towed unit + any load on it (p. 3-1).

numberItems.stem: Where is a tire's load rating — the most weight it can safely carry at a stated pressure — shown?
options: On the bill of lading
On the side of each tire
Only in the vehicle's owner's manual
numberItems.explanation: Tire load is the maximum safe weight a tire can carry at a specified pressure; it is stated on the side of each tire (p. 3-2).

numberItems.stem: Why does a bridge formula allow **less** weight on axles that are closer together?
options: To prevent overloading bridges and roadways
To give the drive wheels more traction
Because closely spaced axles make steering harder
numberItems.explanation: A bridge formula permits less maximum axle weight for axles that are closer together, to prevent overloading bridges and roadways (p. 3-2).

numberItems.stem: In which situations may it be unsafe to drive at the legal maximum weight?
options: At night and on city streets
Never — a legal weight is always a safe weight
In bad weather and in the mountains
numberItems.explanation: During bad weather or in mountains, it may not be safe to operate at legal maximum weights (p. 3-2).

numberItems.stem: Cargo was loaded too far to the rear, so the front axle is under-loaded. What can happen?
options: Hard steering and damage to the steering axle and tires
The steering axle may be too light to steer safely
Nothing, as long as the gross weight is legal
numberItems.explanation: Under-loaded front axles (weight shifted too far to the rear) can make the steering axle too light to steer safely. Too MUCH front weight causes hard steering (p. 3-2).

numberItems.stem: Which describes **blocking**?
options: It is fitted snugly against the front, back and/or sides of the cargo and fastened to the deck to keep it from sliding
It runs from the upper part of the cargo down to the floor and/or walls
It is a cover that protects the cargo from weather
numberItems.explanation: Blocking is used in the front, back and/or sides of cargo, shaped to fit snugly and secured to the deck, to keep it from sliding. The second option describes bracing (p. 3-2).

numberItems.stem: You are securing a heavy machine on a flatbed. The combined (aggregate) working load limit of your tie-downs must be at least:
options: 1½ times the weight of the machine
½ the weight of the machine
The same as the weight of the machine
numberItems.explanation: Federal rules require the aggregate working load limit of the securement system to be at least ½ the weight of the cargo; some practice banks wrongly say 1½ times (p. 3-3).

numberItems.stem: A small crate only a few feet long is on a flatbed. What is the minimum number of tie-downs?
numberItems.explanation: Use at least 1 tie-down per 10 feet of cargo, and no matter how small the cargo, at least 2 tie-downs (p. 3-3).

numberItems.stem: What are the 2 basic reasons for covering cargo?
options: To hide the cargo from thieves and reduce wind drag
To protect people from spilled cargo and to protect the cargo from weather
To keep the cargo cool and to meet placard rules
numberItems.explanation: There are 2 basic reasons for covering cargo: to protect people from spilled cargo and to protect the cargo from weather (p. 3-3).

numberItems.stem: Rules for loading and securing logs, metal coils, concrete pipe and large boulders are found in:
numberItems.explanation: Securement rules for these special commodities are contained in CFR Title 49 §393. CVC §23114 covers spilling loads; §25100 covers wide-load lamps (pp. 3-3–3-5).

numberItems.stem: [CA] It is illegal for any part of a load to spill, blow or sift from a vehicle. What are the only exceptions?
options: Clear water and feathers from live birds
Sand and small gravel
Light trash such as paper
numberItems.explanation: The exceptions are clear water or feathers from live birds (CVC §§23114, 23115; p. 3-4).

numberItems.stem: [CA] You are hauling crushed rock. How must the load be carried?
options: Heaped above the upper edge, as long as it is tarped
In the cargo area, at least 12 inches below the upper edge
In the cargo area, 6 inches below the upper edge
numberItems.explanation: Aggregate material must be carried in the cargo area and be 6 inches below the upper edge (CVC §23114; p. 3-4).

numberItems.stem: [CA] A vehicle hauling aggregate material (sand, gravel, rock) must be equipped with:
options: A red flag at the rear of the load
Seals on any unloading openings, splash flaps behind every tire or set of tires, and fenders
Placards on all four sides
numberItems.explanation: Aggregate haulers need seals on openings used to empty the load, splash flaps behind every tire or set of tires, and fenders (p. 3-4).

numberItems.stem: [CA] Who issues the special transit permits needed for over-length, over-width or overweight loads in California?
options: Caltrans
The DMV
The shipper
numberItems.explanation: Oversized loads require special transit permits — issued by Caltrans in California (p. 3-4).

numberItems.stem: [CA] Your vehicle and load are over 80 inches wide. What lamps go on the side of the projecting load?
options: Red at the front and amber at the rear
Amber at both the front and the rear
Amber at the front and red at the rear
numberItems.explanation: A vehicle and load over 80 inches wide needs an amber combination clearance/side-marker lamp at the front of the projection and a red one at the rear (p. 3-5).

numberItems.stem: [CA] The alternative (single-lamp) rule for a wide projection applies only if the projection extends no more than how far from front to rear?
options: 3 feet
4 feet
1 foot
numberItems.explanation: If the over-width projection extends no more than 3 feet front to rear, a single amber (near front) or red (near rear) lamp may be used (CVC §25100; p. 3-5).

numberItems.stem: [CA] How far past the rear of the body must a load extend before you must flag the end of it?
options: 3 feet or more
4 feet (48 inches) or more
1 foot or more
numberItems.explanation: A load extending 4 feet (48 inches) or more past the rear needs a solid red or fluorescent orange flag at least 12 inches square at the end (p. 3-5).

numberItems.stem: [CA] After dark, you haul pipe that sticks out 5 feet past the rear. Besides the flag, what lights are required at the end of the load?
options: One amber light visible 300 feet to the front and rear
2 lit red lights visible 300 feet to the rear
2 lit red lights visible 500 feet to the side and rear
numberItems.explanation: During darkness, a rear projection needs 2 lit red lights at the end of the load, visible 500 feet to the side and rear (CVC §24604; p. 3-5).

numberItems.stem: [CA] At night, your load extends 1 foot or more to the **left**. What do you need?
options: An amber light on the far left of the load, visible at least 300 feet to the front and rear
2 lit red lights visible 500 feet to the side and rear
Only a red flag at least 12 inches square
numberItems.explanation: A load extending 1 foot or more to the left needs an amber light on the extreme left side, visible at least 300 feet front and rear during darkness (p. 3-5).

numberItems.stem: [CA] A load extends **more than 120 inches**. What lamps are required?
options: An amber lamp at the front and a red lamp at the rear, each visible at least 500 feet
A red lamp at the front and an amber lamp at the rear, each visible at least 300 feet
An amber lamp at the front and a red lamp at the rear, each visible at least 300 feet
numberItems.explanation: If the load extends more than 120 inches, there must be an amber lamp at the front and a red lamp at the rear, each visible at least 300 feet (p. 3-5).

numberItems.stem: [CA] In daylight, a vehicle **wider than 102 inches** must display:
options: A red or fluorescent flag at least 18 inches square at the left rear only
A red or fluorescent flag at least 12 inches square at the left front and left rear
An amber lamp at the widest point
numberItems.explanation: A vehicle wider than 102 inches must display a red or fluorescent flag not less than 12 inches square at the left front and left rear during daylight (CVC §25104; p. 3-5).
